structured_output.hypothesis: If domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species, then the dog genome should show ancestry from two or more separate wild Canis species. Dogs would then not form a single clade nested within one species, Canis lupus.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using the dog reference assembly as the dog reference, compare it with public whole-genome data from wolves, coyotes, golden jackals and other wild canids. The claim is supported if either of two things holds. (a) Dog autosomal ancestry shows at least 25% of non-wolf-derived ancestry from a distinct wild species (e.g. coyote or golden jackal), by D-statistic/f4 or ADMIXTURE, with Z>3. (b) Dog lineages are polyphyletic, with different breeds branching inside two or more different wild species in a genome-wide tree, with bootstrap support of at least 90%.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if dogs form a single monophyletic clade (bootstrap at least 90%) nested within Canis lupus. It is also refuted if at least 95% of dog ancestry traces to wolf lineages and any ancestry from other wild Canis species is below 5%, or is indistinguishable from later admixture (Z<3).
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'wild species' is read as a modern biological species or deeply divergent lineage (Canis lupus, C. latrans, C. aureus and similar). 'Descended from' is read as the origin of the bulk of genome-wide ancestry, not later gene flow after domestication. Darwin worded the claim as probable and said it was based on geographical and other considerations. The test is therefore whether the genome gives a clearly better fit to multiple-species origin than to a single-species origin. Modern genomics has reinterpreted wolves as one species (C. lupus), so the multi-species reading predicts ancestry from species beyond the wolf. The dataset is the NCBI dog reference genome assembly. It supplies the coordinate framework and the sequence for comparisons with other canid assemblies and reads in NCBI. The fields used are the assembly FASTA, its annotation, and linked canid assemblies and SRA runs.

dataset.why_it_fits: It is a public, downloadable reference genome for the domestic dog. It is the standard coordinate system for comparing dog genomes with wolf, coyote and jackal genomes, which lets ancestry be tested directly with D-statistics and phylogenies. NCBI Datasets offers the FASTA and annotation for download and an API.
